items.answer: A head-mounted display (HMD) is a wearable, mobile visual display that integrates electronic, optical, mechanical, and audio components and uses one or two small screens directly in front of the user's eyes to place images for monoscopic or stereoscopic viewing. It can be non-see-through, optical see-through, or video see-through.
Field of view (FOV) is an angular measure of the region visible to the eye at a single point in time, and in virtual reality it is the amount of virtual environment visible.
Three-dimensional audio is specialized audio that gives a sense of where sounds are coming from, with speakers fixed in space or moving with the head.

Augmented reality (AR) is an enhanced version of reality created by technology, in which computer-generated digital content is overlaid on the real world in real time and registered in 3D, so the user perceives and interacts with the enhanced environment.

Virtual reality (VR) is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which replaces the user's sense of reality without requiring the physical existence of objects or places.

An augmented reality system is a system with four required characteristics: it enhances the real world with computer-generated digital content registered in 3D, that content is experienced through the user's sensory organs, and it supports real-time interaction with that content in the enhanced environment.

questions.question: Which term names a category of AR hardware rather than a specific product?
options: Microsoft HoloLens
Google Glass
Spatial augmented reality
Vuzix Blade Glasses
questions.explanation: Spatial augmented reality is one of the AR hardware categories. Microsoft HoloLens, Google Glass, and Vuzix Blade Glasses are named products that belong to other categories.

questions.question: Why can projection keyboards and interactive projectors be counted in two AR hardware categories?
options: They appear as examples of both headsets and smart glasses
They appear as examples of both handheld devices and projection-based systems
They appear as examples of both head-up displays and AR contact lenses
They appear as examples of both projection-based systems and spatial augmented reality
questions.explanation: Projection keyboards and interactive projectors are listed under both projection-based systems and spatial AR. The other pairings mix unrelated AR hardware categories.

questions.question: Which AR hardware category is described as the latest technology being explored for AR systems?
options: AR head-up displays
AR contact lenses
AR headsets
AR smart glasses
questions.explanation: AR contact lenses are the newest AR hardware idea, with ongoing research. The other categories are established AR hardware types rather than the latest exploratory technology.

questions.question: Which application domain is listed for handheld AR devices but not for AR headsets and smart glasses?
options: Healthcare
E-commerce
Retail
Manufacturing
questions.explanation: Handheld AR devices include e-commerce among their application domains, while headsets and smart glasses do not. Healthcare and manufacturing belong to headsets and smart glasses, and retail is shared by both.

data.text: Augmented reality hardware is described through its main device categories, each with representative examples. Head-up displays and contact lenses are then placed in their typical contexts: cars and active research. The application domains connect each hardware category to the fields where it is used.
points: Augmented reality hardware is grouped into headsets and glasses, handheld devices, projection-based systems, spatial AR, head-up displays, and contact lenses.
Examples include HoloLens, smart glasses, smartphones, interactive projectors, AR sandboxes, and projection keyboards, with overlap between projection-based and spatial AR.
AR head-up displays are typically found in cars.
AR contact lenses are the latest technology being explored for AR systems, with ongoing research.
AR hardware categories have different application domains, including education, healthcare, retail, industrial applications, and gaming.

questions.question: Compared with a VR headset, what is a typical characteristic of an AR headset?
options: A lighter form factor that resembles standard eyeglasses
A fully synthetic view that replaces the real-world view
A narrower view that relies less on depth sensing
A wider view that keeps real-world content visible
questions.explanation: AR headsets typically present real-world content together with added digital content and often provide a wider field of view. VR headsets can have fewer components because they do not need to preserve the real-world view.

questions.question: What is typical of cameras and depth sensors in an AR headset?
options: They are often built in, and some may also be present in VR headsets
They are often built in, and they are typical of smart glasses rather than headsets
They are often built in, and they replace the real-world view
They are often built in, but they are absent from VR headsets
questions.explanation: AR headsets typically include built-in sensors such as cameras and depth sensors, but the same kinds of sensors may also appear in VR headsets. They do not replace the real-world view, which is the defining role of VR display content.

questions.question: What does the Microsoft HoloLens present to the user?
options: A view of high-definition holograms integrated into the real world
A view of fully computer-generated content that replaces the real world
A view of heads-up display information intended for automobile use
A view of projection-based keyboard controls for industrial design
questions.explanation: The HoloLens integrates high-definition holograms or digital content with the real-world view seen through its special glasses. It is not a fully virtual display, projection keyboard, or automotive heads-up display.

questions.question: Which set describes interaction in the Microsoft HoloLens?
options: Trackpad, microphone, and camera
Eye movements, voice commands, and hand gestures
Touchpad, button, and haptic feedback
Joystick, mouse, and keyboard
questions.explanation: Interaction in the HoloLens is through detected eye movements, voice commands, and hand gestures. The other options list components or input devices that are not the stated interaction methods for this headset.

data.text: Augmented reality headsets are generally larger, more immersive, and have a wider field of view than virtual reality headsets, and they typically include built-in sensors such as cameras and depth sensors. The Microsoft HoloLens is an example of such AR hardware: it has more components than many VR headsets, projects digital content into the real-world view, and supports eye, voice, and hand-based interaction.
points: Generally, augmented reality headsets are larger, more immersive, and have a wider field of view.
Augmented reality headsets typically include built-in sensors, often cameras and depth sensors, which may also be in virtual reality headsets.
Microsoft HoloLens is an augmented reality headset with more components than virtual reality headsets, including cameras and a projector.
Microsoft HoloLens integrates high-definition digital holograms with the real-world view through its special glasses.
Microsoft HoloLens interaction uses eye movements, voice commands, and hand motions, which the device detects.

questions.question: Which wearable AR category typically provides full 3D holograms rather than simpler heads-up overlays?
options: The AR headset category
The spatial AR category
The handheld AR category
The AR smart-glasses category
questions.explanation: AR headsets contain more components, sensors, and projectors, which supports full 3D holograms, while AR smart glasses usually show simpler overlay content.

questions.question: What makes AR smart glasses more comfortable than AR headsets for extended periods?
options: Their heavier, headset-like design
Their projector-based, room-scale design
Their camera-overlay, handheld design
Their lighter, eyeglass-like design
questions.explanation: AR smart glasses are lighter, eyeglass-like wearables, which makes them more comfortable to wear for longer than more powerful AR headsets.

questions.question: What display method do handheld AR devices typically use?
options: Showing digital content on a see-through lens
Overlaying digital content on a live camera view
Projecting digital content onto physical objects
Replacing the real view with a virtual environment
questions.explanation: A handheld AR device captures a live real-world image with its own camera and displays digital content overlaid on that live view.

questions.question: What two operational approaches are typically used by handheld AR devices?
options: Marker-based and markerless AR
Voice-based and touch-based AR
Projector-based and camera-based AR
Headset-based and glasses-based AR
questions.explanation: Handheld AR devices typically rely on marker-based AR and markerless AR.

data.text: AR hardware includes smart glasses and handheld devices. AR smart glasses are lighter and less immersive than AR headsets, so they provide simpler heads-up overlays rather than full 3D holograms; examples such as Google Glass and Vuzix Blade combine displays, sensors, and input features. Handheld AR devices, especially smartphones and tablets, are the most common and accessible form, capturing the real world with a camera and adding digital content through marker-based or markerless AR.
points: AR smart glasses are lighter, less immersive, smaller-field-of-view, and less powerful than AR headsets, but more comfortable for extended wear.
AR smart glasses show simpler heads-up overlays, not full 3D holograms, because AR headsets have more components.
AR smart glasses such as Google Glass and Vuzix Blade include cameras, displays or projectors, sensors, and input controls.
Handheld AR devices are smartphones or tablets, the most common and accessible AR devices.
Handheld AR devices capture a live real-world view, overlay digital content, and use marker-based or markerless AR.

activities.title: Order the steps in generating a handheld augmented reality view

items.title: Order the steps in generating a handheld augmented reality view
steps: The device captures a live real-world image with its camera
The device displays the captured image on its screen
The device overlays digital content on the live real-world view

questions.question: What is a defining feature of a spatial augmented reality device?
options: Its display element is a head-mounted screen worn by the user
Its display element is a transparent visor mounted for the user
Its display element is not tied to or held by the user
Its display element is a handheld screen held by the user
questions.explanation: Spatial augmented reality displays are placed in the environment and project digital content onto physical objects, so the display is not worn, held, or otherwise tied to an individual user. Head-mounted, handheld, or visor-mounted displays remain tied to the person using them.

questions.question: Why can a spatial augmented reality system support several users interacting with the same content?
options: The content is triggered by a marker seen by each user
The content is rendered in a personal display worn by each user
The content is captured on a handheld camera held by each user
The content is augmented onto one physical object used by each user
questions.explanation: In spatial augmented reality, the shared digital content is augmented onto a physical object, so several people can interact with that same content at the same time. With headsets, glasses, or handheld devices, each user interacts only with the content shown on that user's own device.

questions.question: What must a spatial augmented reality system understand for the mixed content to look seamless?
options: The geometry and lighting conditions of the physical environment
The marker positions and target orientations of the physical environment
The user's head pose and eye direction relative to the physical environment
The handheld camera's live view and overlay alignment with the physical environment
questions.explanation: Seamless mixing requires the system to match virtual content to the shape and lighting of the real space. That understanding can come from depth sensors or computer vision techniques included in the system.

questions.question: What makes the projected topographic map in an air sandbox change in real time?
options: Movement of the sand or gestures tracked by a sensor
Rotation or zooming of a projected image tracked by a sensor
A marker's position in a captured view tracked by a sensor
Finger positions on a flat surface tracked by a sensor
questions.explanation: An air sandbox uses a projector and a sensor, such as a 3D camera, to show a map on sand and update it when users move the sand or make gestures. The other options describe different spatial AR examples rather than the air sandbox mechanism.

data.text: Spatial AR is the projector-based, shared-space category of AR: virtual content is placed on physical objects in the real environment, so several users can interact with it at once. To make that content feel coexisting, systems must understand the environment's geometry and lighting, usually through depth sensors or computer vision. Representative examples include interactive projectors, air sandboxes, projection keyboards, and projection mapping, which differ in whether they project onto surfaces, sand, or 3D space. These systems are used in education, art, medicine, industry, museums, and entertainment.
points: Spatial AR devices are projector-based, room-scale systems that place virtual content on physical objects, not the user's view.
Their non-held displays can provide more natural interfaces and let multiple users interact with the same content.
Spatial AR is used in domains such as education, art, medicine, industry, museums, and entertainment.
Projection-based and spatial AR are generally similar ideas, needing geometry and lighting understanding via sensors or computer vision.
Examples include interactive projectors, air sandboxes, projection keyboards, and projection mapping, projecting interactive surfaces or 3D space.

questions.question: Which surface is normally used by a head-up display in cars and aircraft?
options: an opaque dashboard panel
a tabletop projection surface
a handheld tablet or phone
a transparent screen or visor
questions.explanation: A head-up display projects images onto a transparent surface, usually a screen or visor, so the user can see the content while viewing the real world.

questions.question: How do AR contact lenses deliver digital information to the wearer?
options: by projecting it onto a visor in front of the face
by projecting it onto a physical object in the room
by replacing the real view with a virtual scene
by superimposing it directly on the eye-mounted wearable
questions.explanation: AR contact lenses superimpose digital images or information directly on the lens worn on the eye, rather than projecting it onto an external object or replacing the real view.

questions.question: What makes AR contact lenses different from many other AR display devices?
options: They use projectors to display content on physical objects in the room
They are bulky and are held in the hand
They are not visible to outsiders and sit like a regular contact lens
They are commonly used in cars and aircraft for long periods
questions.explanation: AR contact lenses are placed directly on the eye like a regular contact lens and are not visible to outsiders, unlike many bulky or held AR devices.

questions.question: What open user issue is associated with AR contact lenses?
options: They may hide the real world behind an opaque image
They may affect normal behavior or cause some sort of sickness
They may become too bulky to keep on the eye
They may require markers in the environment to update the image
questions.explanation: The effect of AR contact lenses is not well known, because seeing lots of changing information directly in front of the eyes may affect normal behavior or cause some sort of sickness.

data.text: Head-up displays and AR contact lenses complete the AR display categories. Head-up displays project images onto transparent surfaces and are commonly used in cars and aircraft. AR contact lenses contrast with bulkier AR hardware as tiny future wearables that can place digital information directly on the eye and may include miniaturized electronic components. Their possible usefulness is set against the unresolved concern that constantly changing visual information may affect users or cause sickness.
points: A head-up display projects images onto a transparent surface; ideally only content is visible, though borders or shades may be.
Head-up displays are commonly used in cars and aircraft.
Some AR hardware is bulky or hard to hold, while AR contact lenses are tiny future wearables.
AR contact lenses superimpose digital information directly on the lens and may carry miniaturized display, imaging, wireless, and motion components.
AR contact lenses may show and let users change information, but their effects are not well known and may cause sickness.

items.reason: A tilt mechanism, nose pad and depth camera are components of the Microsoft HoloLens, whereas a gyroscope is a component of Google Glass.

questions.question: Why can augmented reality headsets provide more immersive three-dimensional holographic content than augmented reality smart glasses?
questions.reference_answer: Augmented reality headsets can provide more immersive three-dimensional holographic content because they generally have a wider field of view and contain more components, sensors, and projectors. They are generally larger and more immersive than smart glasses. Smart glasses are lighter, less powerful, and usually have a smaller field of view, so they provide simpler head-up-display-type overlays.

questions.question: Why can a virtual reality headset have fewer components than an augmented reality headset such as the Microsoft HoloLens?
questions.reference_answer: A virtual reality headset can have fewer components because it does not need to provide a real-world view. It replaces the user's sense of reality rather than altering perception of the real world. By contrast, the Microsoft HoloLens includes special glasses that project digital content onto the regular real-world view, along with a camera, depth cameras, and a projector.

questions.question: Why can a spatial augmented reality system let several users interact with the same digital content, while head-mounted displays, smart glasses, and handheld devices do not?
questions.reference_answer: A spatial augmented reality system can let several users interact with the same digital content because its display is placed on shared physical objects in the real world, not tied to one user. These systems typically use projectors to augment physical objects, and the augmented content can therefore be used by multiple users at once. Headsets, glasses, and handheld devices instead show content only in the user's own view or on the user's own screen.

questions.question: Why might augmented reality contact lenses remain a future technology even though they can place digital information directly in the wearer's field of vision?
questions.reference_answer: Augmented reality contact lenses remain a future technology because their effect on users is not well known or researched. They are very small, can be placed on the eye like regular contact lenses, and can superimpose digital images or information directly onto the wearer's field of vision. However, a lot of changing information directly in front of the eyes may affect normal behavior or cause some sort of sickness.
